The Gray hawk (Buteo plagiatus) is a medium-sized raptor inhabiting arid woodlands and riparian corridors from the southwestern United States through Central America. As an altricial species with a relatively protracted developmental period, neonatal chicks emerge from calcareous eggs after an incubation period of approximately 32 days [ab = approximately 32 days] when held at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. The initial wet weight at hatching is 43.2 grams [Ww0 = 43.2 grams], a modest mass that reflects the energetic constraints of yolk-dependent development in a species occupying seasonal environments. This neo-natal body mass, recorded from captive breeding colonies in southern Arizona, is consistent with values documented for other Buteo species of similar body size. The chicks are entirely dependent on biparental provisioning during the first weeks post-hatching, with both parents providing prey items to the nestling as the young undergo rapid feather development and somatic growth.

During the nestling period, the young Gray hawk experiences a phase of rapid mass gain that continues until fledging. Under typical thermal conditions approximating 40 °C [T = 40 °C], which correspond to the upper end of ambient temperatures experienced during the breeding season in its range, fledging occurs at 42 days after hatching [tx = 42 days after hatching]. This milestone, marking the achievement of flight feather maturation and first flight, is a critical transition in the life cycle, after which the fledgling remains near the nest for several additional weeks while still receiving some parental provisioning. The timing of nest departure in this species appears to be correlated with local prey abundance, though the value reported from field studies in Sonora, Mexico, indicates a consistent developmental schedule under favorable conditions. The relatively rapid wing feather development compared to other Buteo species may be an adaptation to the seasonal monsoon rains that characterize much of its range.

Puberty, characterized by the onset of gonadal maturation and gametogenesis, occurs considerably later than fledging in the Gray hawk. Based on longitudinal studies of marked individuals in the wild, sexual maturity is attained at 126 days after hatching [tp = 126 days after hatching] at an ambient temperature regime of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This protracted period between fledging and reproductive activation reflects the considerable time required for full somatic development and the acquisition of hunting proficiency necessary for successful territory establishment. Young birds in their first year often wander extensively before settling, and the relatively late onset of puberty may also be influenced by the competitive environment for nesting territories along riparian corridors. Comparative data from captive populations suggest that nutritional condition during the juvenile stage can accelerate or delay this maturational timeline, though the field-based estimate remains the standard reference for wild individuals.

First reproduction, defined as the first successful breeding attempt and initiation of a clutch, is delayed until approximately 730 days after hatching [tR = approximately 730 days after hatching] under the same thermal conditions of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This two-year delay from hatching to first brood is typical of medium-sized accipitrid raptors and reflects the extended period required for territory acquisition, pair formation, and the refinement of foraging skills. Once a nesting territory is secured, females typically produce a single clutch per year, with each clutch containing 1 to 5 eggs. This relatively low fecundity, combined with the deferred age at first reproduction, results in a modest annual reproductive output that is compensated by high adult survival rates. The species thus aligns with a slow life-history strategy common among tropical and subtropical raptors, where environmental predictability and competition for limited nesting sites favor investment in self-maintenance over high fecundity.

Adult body mass shows pronounced sexual size dimorphism in the Gray hawk, a common pattern among raptorial birds. Female ultimate wet weight reaches 624 grams [Wwi = 624 grams], while the corresponding value for males is 429.75 grams [Wwi = 429.75 grams], representing a female-biased mass ratio of approximately 1.45. This dimorphism is reflected in the species' foraging ecology, where females typically take larger prey items while males provision the nest during early incubation. Maximum recorded longevity in the wild, derived from banding returns and long-term monitoring programs, is estimated at 30.7 years [am = 30.7 years] under ambient field temperatures approximating 40 °C [T = 40 °C], a lifespan that ranks among the highest documented for medium-sized Buteo species. This extended lifespan, combined with the single annual clutch and relatively small clutch sizes, underscores a conservative life-history strategy in which adult survival and iteroparity compensate for low annual fecundity. The relatively high adult survivorship likely reflects the species' position as a generalist predator with access to diverse prey throughout the year.
